The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspective from Krish Patel, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Perspective Back to Top Krish Patel, MD Krish Patel, MD For more than 2 decades, R-CHOP has been the global standard of care for newly diagnosed patients with DLBCL, leading to cure in about 60% of patients. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial.
Perspective from Krish Patel, MD
Krish Patel, MD
The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed.
diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago.
The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting.
Georg Lenz
“I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.”
Georg Lenz, MD
An unmet need
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases.
R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades.
However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease.
“We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said.
Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant.
The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL.
Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas.
The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL.
All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment.
Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles.
PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints.
‘Good chance’ for cure
Median follow-up reached 35.2 months.
The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed.
The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin.
Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%).
“Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.”
Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%).
An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival.
“We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said.
‘Manageable’ toxicities
The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events.
Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%).
More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%).
Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles.
“The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.”
Evolving treatment landscape
The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment.
The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting.
The New England Journal of Medicine
Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment.
The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL.
epcoritamab
The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said.
“The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out.
“Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.”

CHICAGO — The bispecific antibody linvoseltamab exhibited rapid clinical activity among patients with relapsed or refractory systemic light chain amyloidosis, according to phase 1/phase 2 trial results presented at ASCO Annual Meeting. All 20 treated patients achieved objective response and 18 achieved hematologic complete response. Data derived from Wechalekar AD, et al. Abstract 7502. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. Linvoseltamab (Lynozyfic, Regeneron) also exhibited what researchers characterized as a manageable safety profile, with no dose-limiting toxicities reported. Hans C. Lee “The safety profile is very encouraging, and to see rapid and deep hematologic responses is unprecedented in this patient population,” Hans C. Lee, MD, director of myeloma research at Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told Healio. “This could have tremendous implications for previously treated light chain amyloidosis — and possibly down the road for newly diagnosed patients.” ‘Significant unmet need’ Light chain (AL) amyloidosis — a rare systemic plasma cell disorder — results in pathogenic secretion of light chain fibrils that gather in organs such as the heart or kidneys. This can lead to end-organ damage, other significant morbidity or death. Approximately 43% of all patients with AL amyloidosis survive 5 years and about 27% live 10 years. The CD38-targeted antibody daratumumab (Darzalex, Johson & Johnson) in combination with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone is approved for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis. However, no therapies are approved for relapsed or refractory disease; consequently, drugs that are efficacious for treatment of multiple myeloma often are used off-label. “Oftentimes these approaches do not lead to rapid and deep responses,” Lee said. “We are trying to target plasma cells effectively, but it also is imperative to decrease the production and organ deposition of the light chain fibrils as quickly as possible, so there is a significant unmet need in this setting.” Linvoseltamab, a bispecific B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CD3 T-cell engager, is approved for treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma who received at least four previous therapies. In the LINKER-AL2 trial, Lee and colleagues assessed the safety and efficacy of linvoseltamab monotherapy for patients with relapsed or refractory systemic AL amyloidosis. ‘Encouraged and excited’ Trial participants received step-up doses of IV linvoseltamab — 5 mg on day 1 and 25 mg on day 8 — of cycle 0. They received full subcutaneous doses — either 80 mg or 240 mg — once weekly for two 28-day cycles, followed by once every 4 weeks in cycles 3 through 12. Dose-limiting toxicities within 28 days of the first full dose served as the primary endpoint of the phase 1 portion of the trial. Secondary endpoints included hematologic complete response — assessed by free light chain ratio and absence of amyloidogenic light chains — along with rates of objective response, very good partial response or better, and time to response. Investigators also evaluated additional safety outcomes. Twenty patients (median age, 64 years) — 60% of whom had received prior daratumumab — received treatment. Seven received 80 mg full doses and 13 received 240 mg doses. Median follow-up reached 9.5 weeks. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred. All patients experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, and 65% experienced grade 3 or higher events. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events — which occurred primarily during step-up dosing — included cytokine release syndrome (grade 1, 35%; grade 2, 15%) and infusion-related reactions (35%, all grade 1/grade 2). Twenty-five percent of patients developed grade 3 or higher infections. One patient developed grade 1 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. Researchers reported one case of grade 5 ventricular fibrillation in a patient with pre-existing coronary artery disease in the context of coronary artery stent placement, and one case of grade 5 sudden cardiac death in a patient with cardiac amyloidosis. Investigators deemed both events unrelated to linvoseltamab. “These patients often are quite frail because they have organ involvement, so the safety profile overall is very encouraging,” Lee said. All 20 patients achieved very good partial response or better. Eighteen patients (90%) achieved hematologic complete response. Median time to complete hematologic response was about 1.5 months, and median time to normalization of involved free light chain — defined as less than 20 mg/L — was 15 days. This translated into what Lee called “encouraging organ responses,” with a 73% renal response rate and 50% cardiac response rate. Investigators expect these responses could deepen with longer follow-up, he added. Due to the encouraging phase 1 results, researchers will move forward with the phase 2 portion of the LINKER-AL2 trial. A larger cohort of patients with relapsed or refractory AL amyloidosis will be enrolled and randomly assigned to linvoseltamab at either the 80 mg or 240 mg dose. That study will have “potential registrational intent,” Lee said. “We are encouraged and excited by the efficacy results so far,” Lee said. “They highlight how BCMA bispecific antibodies will be an important modality of therapy for this patient population moving forward. Because this is an off-the-shelf therapy, it can be accessible to patients regardless of whether they are treated at large urban centers or smaller community practices.” For more information: Hans C. Light chain (AL) amyloidosis — a rare systemic plasma cell disorder — results in pathogenic secretion of light chain fibrils that gather in organs such as the heart or kidneys. This can lead to end-organ damage, other significant morbidity or death.
Light chain (AL) amyloidosis
Approximately 43% of all patients with AL amyloidosis survive 5 years and about 27% live 10 years.
The CD38-targeted antibody daratumumab (Darzalex, Johson & Johnson) in combination with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone is approved for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis. However, no therapies are approved for relapsed or refractory disease; consequently, drugs that are efficacious for treatment of multiple myeloma often are used off-label.
daratumumab (Darzalex, Johson & Johnson)
“Oftentimes these approaches do not lead to rapid and deep responses,” Lee said. “We are trying to target plasma cells effectively, but it also is imperative to decrease the production and organ deposition of the light chain fibrils as quickly as possible, so there is a significant unmet need in this setting.”
Linvoseltamab, a bispecific B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CD3 T-cell engager, is approved for treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma who received at least four previous therapies.
In the LINKER-AL2 trial, Lee and colleagues assessed the safety and efficacy of linvoseltamab monotherapy for patients with relapsed or refractory systemic AL amyloidosis.
‘Encouraged and excited’
Trial participants received step-up doses of IV linvoseltamab — 5 mg on day 1 and 25 mg on day 8 — of cycle 0.
They received full subcutaneous doses — either 80 mg or 240 mg — once weekly for two 28-day cycles, followed by once every 4 weeks in cycles 3 through 12.
Dose-limiting toxicities within 28 days of the first full dose served as the primary endpoint of the phase 1 portion of the trial. Secondary endpoints included hematologic complete response — assessed by free light chain ratio and absence of amyloidogenic light chains — along with rates of objective response, very good partial response or better, and time to response. Investigators also evaluated additional safety outcomes.
Twenty patients (median age, 64 years) — 60% of whom had received prior daratumumab — received treatment. Seven received 80 mg full doses and 13 received 240 mg doses.
Median follow-up reached 9.5 weeks.
All patients experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, and 65% experienced grade 3 or higher events.
The most common treatment-emergent adverse events — which occurred primarily during step-up dosing — included cytokine release syndrome (grade 1, 35%; grade 2, 15%) and infusion-related reactions (35%, all grade 1/grade 2). Twenty-five percent of patients developed grade 3 or higher infections. One patient developed grade 1 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome.
Researchers reported one case of grade 5 ventricular fibrillation in a patient with pre-existing coronary artery disease in the context of coronary artery stent placement, and one case of grade 5 sudden cardiac death in a patient with cardiac amyloidosis. Investigators deemed both events unrelated to linvoseltamab.
“These patients often are quite frail because they have organ involvement, so the safety profile overall is very encouraging,” Lee said.
All 20 patients achieved very good partial response or better. Eighteen patients (90%) achieved hematologic complete response. Median time to complete hematologic response was about 1.5 months, and median time to normalization of involved free light chain — defined as less than 20 mg/L — was 15 days.
This translated into what Lee called “encouraging organ responses,” with a 73% renal response rate and 50% cardiac response rate. Investigators expect these responses could deepen with longer follow-up, he added.
Due to the encouraging phase 1 results, researchers will move forward with the phase 2 portion of the LINKER-AL2 trial. A larger cohort of patients with relapsed or refractory AL amyloidosis will be enrolled and randomly assigned to linvoseltamab at either the 80 mg or 240 mg dose.
That study will have “potential registrational intent,” Lee said.
“We are encouraged and excited by the efficacy results so far,” Lee said. “They highlight how BCMA bispecific antibodies will be an important modality of therapy for this patient population moving forward. Because this is an off-the-shelf therapy, it can be accessible to patients regardless of whether they are treated at large urban centers or smaller community practices.”
